Messages.Author: Jay Kristoff
Messages.Body:
Hi folks,
I would like to clarify some things about the article I wrote for
John Eno's blog:
http://enoplay.blogspot.com/2010/07/origins-special-report-us-championships.html
.

The conversation I had with James was made prior to the time when
the finalists were gathered
to pick seating. That conversation was held in public (at one of the
tables in the V:TES area), but
away from most of the other players. I understand now that it was a
bad idea to have that conversation
away from most of the other V:TES players. The caution with which I
spoke to James was not to aid in our secrecy, but in order to protect
my existence in the final round. As alpha members of the same
playgroup, James and I have a history of ruining each other's game
from across the table. When playing his Lutz/Maris Streck deck, James
often "whores out" intercept via Maris to thwart my actions across the
table. The primary reason I spoke with James was to try to get him to
not screw me too early in the round. My talk of not letting Hugh win
was a smokescreen that really meant "please leave me alone". At no
point was I interested in any outcome of the US Championship final
that did not involve me winning.
In writing my article for the State of Play blog, I chose to include
my anti-Hugh talk as theme of the article to provide what I thought
would be compelling reading, and a sort of "rah-rah", pep rally
enthusiasm. My article seems to have been compelling, but in a way I
had not envisioned :)
At the time my conversation with James I did not think I was
cheating (or else I wouldn't have done it). A week later I did not
think of it as cheating (or else I wouldn't have written about it).
After the fallout from my article I'm not sure. I do see the
arrangement of seating for final rounds as an opportunity for shady
behavior. I would be okay with the V:EKN rules being changed to seat
final rounds randomly.

Jay Kristoff

This is the one thing that bothers me about finals. One player should
not have an out of game advantage over another going into a final.
Yet finishing a game early often results in an advantage as players
can scout the tournament.(see one of many discussions on this).

The Sunday tournament is a great example of that. By the time the
finals rolled around everyone knew Una was at the table. Cylon model
fourteen, or John Eno as you all know him, smartly chose to sit as my
predator since Una plays no pool gain or bounce(or I'd assume that's
why), and if the deck goes off it doesn't matter where you are sitting
because Una rushes you anyways. The only player in the final who had
seen the deck in game was Merlin who faced it the round before. He
chose to sit across from me, a spot he got 1VP and almost two the
round before. All for naught as Mr. Cesewayo taught them the folly of
taking D actions to oust your prey not being conducive to victory.

I've been on both ends of final round seating decisions, but I'd
rather just see them go away and make it random. I don't get to
choose seating position in round 2 or 3 because I'm currently the
highest seed, so why does that change for the finals? It falls into
the same issue I have with rounds being 2 hours and a final switching
to 2.5 or 3 hours. Every round of a tournament(including finals)
should be played under the same rules.

In article <i1h5ik$km1$1...@news.eternal-september.org>,

"Kevin M." <you...@imaspammer.org> wrote:
> I've never seen anyone do this in >100 finals I've witnessed.

We always do this at our tournaments. Well, not really have everyone
give an oral report on their decks, but if there is someone in the final
who doesn't know what everyone is playing, they'll ask the table, and
someone will say "oh, he's got a weenie vote deck" or whatever.

The *biggest* flaw in the seating rules for final games is, for my
money, that there is imperfect distribution of information in terms of
what decks are being played. Some people go into the finals and know
what everyone is playing by virtue of pure luck and having been in games
with everyone else in the finals, and some people might have only seen
one other deck at the table (heck, possibly even no other decks at the
table in a huge tournament). This makes picking seats no better than
random some of the time, and greatly incentivizes scouting tables (which
isn't a problem for me, but some folks seem to think it is bad--I think
scouting is just the only reasonable option if you are using the finals
seating rules we have), just to make sure you know what everyone is
playing in case you get to the finals.

As a result, it makes complete sense to, if you get to the finals and
don't know what decks people are playing, say "Hey. What is Bill using?"
I'll happily tell folks every time if I know.

Agreed. But I'd like to add other considerations.

Even with random finals seating, a player still has an incentive to
try to be top-ranked, because the top-ranked player still has the
substantial advantage that he can play the final to a tie, and still
win the tournament.

Hence, there will still be an incentive to play as well as possible in
the prelims unless:

(1) one is assured of a rank 1 position
(2) one is assured of getting into the finals, but a rank 1 position
is not possible.

Neither of these scenarios seems likely to occur in the ordinary
course of a tournament. Combine them with a realistic opportunity to
propel a colluding buddy into the finals, and it becomes even more
unlikely.

On Jul 14, 5:35 am, Sudden Reversal <sudden.rever...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Well, it seems that the fairest option available and least open to
> possible collusion and the disparity from scouting is that of
> randomised seating for the final.

Yet the current system provides a good, concrete incentive to try and
do as well as you possibly can in the preliminaries--scraping up one
extra VP in some game can mean the difference between top seed and
second seed, which is very significant. Which I think is good.

Honestly, I suspect that the issue of final round seating collusion is
one that is being vastly overblown here; it seems likely that the vast
majority of final rounds have people choosing their seats with no
thought of anything other than what seat gives them the best chance to
win. And throwing out a perfectly good system in the name of
protecting the game from a really small chance of someone trying to
collude in a final round with their seating seems silly.

In terms of imperfect deck knowledge, that is easily solved by virtue
of simply assuming that people are going to scout or get information
from their buddies about what decks everyone is playing, and giving
that official blessing. Nothing in the game changes as a result (as it
is already super simple to scout and get information of people's decks
anyway) except that is one less thing for a hyper-anal judge to have
to worry about.

-Peter

improve his chance of being the winner of the tournament, to throw a

> surprised me. It also intrigued me a bit, because I realized I had no
> proof that he was wrong. I just don't have the hard data, and his

My understanding of "The Top Seed Curse" is such that it is mostly an
anecdotal, not actually supported by data, bit of color (i.e. Jim gets
into the final as Top Seed all the time, but never wins when he is Top
Seed). Yes, Top Seed does not win the final more often than xe does. But
I have no reason to believe that being Top Seed makes you any *less*
likely to win than anyone else.

As noted, I suspect that getting seat choice is a bonus. Being in
everyone's gun sights from the get go is a negative. It probably
balances out. Add in that being Top Seed likely means that you have a
good deck and are a good player, and you probably have a slightly better
chance than average to win the final as Top Seed, but not so much that
it overcomes the reality that there are 4 other players at the table,
all of whom can also win.

> I did not assume Kevin was correct. The "top seed curse" remains
> unproven and still, I suspect, probably wrong (though even if it is,
> it may well be that the top seed advantage is far less than some
> assume). But it was still an intriguing hypothetical that I was

Sure. But all we know from presented data is that Top Seed in a given
final does not win a majority of the time.

The way I see it, it takes away the main drawback of being higher seed
(people sometimes ganging up on you because they know you're higher seed)
while keeping the tie-breaker benefit. It was brought up in response
to some people pointing out that high seed rarely wins.

I like the out-of-the-box thinking and the side benefit: that I imagine
such a setup would encourage everyone to go for the tournament win via
VPs & GW and not gunning to win a tie, as they would be uncertain which
way the tie would resolve.

That's not my experience. I believe top seed to be a good benefit. It
doesn't guarantee victory, but it's still a good benefit. Yes, people gun
for the top seeded player sometimes, but not always. I wouldn't trade not
picking my seat for keeping my (now lessened) advantage a secret,
especially since it wouldn't always be a secret anyway.

> I like the out-of-the-box thinking and the side benefit: that I imagine
> such a setup would encourage everyone to go for the tournament win via
> VPs & GW and not gunning to win a tie, as they would be uncertain which
> way the tie would resolve.

This still doesn't seem like a problem being solved. More like a
"nice-to-have" then. I expect that's not sufficient justification to
change the rules.

Also, if players are "gunning for a tie" and succeeding, it is only due to
massive failure on the part of the other four players at the table who are
all aware that they lose on a tie. If timeouts are a problem, they are
best solved by better (or more situationally aware) players, not better
rules, IMO.

That's the major problem that I have with this line of attack. I too have
been troubled by excessive timeouts in vtes (though mostly in preliminary
rounds). This has been solved to some degree by retraining myself and by
believing that .5 VPs is not a good outcome on any table. My philosophy
now is that a 5% shot at 1 VP is better than a 100% shot at .5. I'm not
sure that this practice has increased overall the number of VPs I'm
taking, but I'm timing out less at least.

Next step: better decks! (any year now)
